result: LabNet is a C++ optimized control layer software designed for time-critical operations and extensibility, leveraging the actor model (specifically SObjectizer) for multithreading and modularity, with a Protobuf-based message protocol supporting multiple client languages.
evaluation: Claims C2-C7 establish LabNet's core architecture and design goals, while C63, C74, and C183 provide the technical rationale for key implementation choices (C++ for speed, actor model for concurrency, SObjectizer as the framework). These are consistently described design decisions and architectural features that form the foundation of the system.

result: LabNet achieves sub-millisecond network communication latencies (0.26-1.01 ms median depending on platform and client language) in basic set/ping tests, with performance comparable across C++, C#, and Python clients and improved performance on RasPi 4 due to 1 GigE networking.
evaluation: Claims C8-C9 state the general performance result, while C76-C84 provide specific quantitative measurements from the 'set out' test across different platforms and languages. Claims C92-C94 provide comparative analysis. The data is internally consistent and supports the conclusion that client language choice has minimal impact on performance for simple operations.

result: LabNet uses 4 kHz polling by default for digital input detection, achieving 0.9±0.19 ms latency while utilizing only 10% of one CPU core, with compiler optimization flags having no measurable effect on performance.
evaluation: Claims C85-C86 describe the polling mechanism, C87-C89 provide quantitative performance data comparing different polling frequencies, and C90-C91 report the compiler optimization finding. The data demonstrates a deliberate design trade-off between latency and CPU utilization, with empirical support for the chosen 4 kHz default.

result: LabNet can monitor and control up to 14 pairs of digital I/O pins simultaneously without latency degradation, processing up to 2,800 total events per second, with the four-core RasPi architecture limiting individual pin throughput to ~200 events/second beyond 4 pin pairs.
evaluation: Claims C10 and C95 state the main result, while C96-C97 and C100-C105 provide detailed quantitative measurements and analysis of the stress test. The explanation of the performance drop at >4 pin pairs (C102-C104) is mechanistically reasonable given the 4-core architecture, though it remains an inference rather than direct measurement.

result: LabNet achieves latencies (0.90±0.19 ms) comparable to locally-executed tools despite network communication: faster than Autopilot (0.93±0.08 ms) and Whisker (~1 ms), similar to pyControl (0.66±0.11 ms), but slower than Bpod (0.1±0.002 ms) which runs at 10 kHz.
evaluation: Claims C106-C109 describe the comparison methodology, C113-C117 provide specific measurements for each tool, and C118 states the conclusion. The comparison is methodologically sound with one important caveat: the comparison tools ran locally without network overhead (C109), giving LabNet a disadvantage. The pyControl result (C115) is validated against published data, strengthening confidence.

result: LabNet implements a distributed system architecture where each RasPi node runs identical software as a server, nodes can be added/removed without reconfiguration, at most one experimental system connects per RasPi, and clients (not LabNet) are responsible for experimental logic.
evaluation: Claims C44-C54 consistently describe the distributed system architecture and division of responsibilities. The design achieves openness and scalability (C45-C46) through uniformity (C48-C49) at the cost of flexibility (C50). The single-connection limitation (C51) is a logical consequence of the one-system-per-RasPi constraint (C50), simplifying resource management.

result: LabNet has been successfully deployed in bat foraging experiments with up to 76 artificial flowers, each containing multiple sensors and actuators, with RFID identification, used in both rainforest field studies and laboratory settings, demonstrating scalability and real-world applicability.
evaluation: Claims C124-C127 describe the experimental system with supporting citations, while C128-C132 detail the technical implementation and network architecture. The progression from earlier systems to current LabNet implementation is well-documented. The citations to published work (Winter and Stich 2005, Nachev et al. 2017, Wintergerst et al. 2021) provide external validation of successful deployment.

result: LabNet has been successfully deployed in rodent behavioral experiments including group-housed mice with automated water dispensers, touchscreen systems for rats integrated with commercial Campden Instruments equipment, and fully custom touchscreen systems for group-housed mice with automated sorting, demonstrating versatility and integration capabilities.
evaluation: Claims C133-C150 describe multiple rodent experimental systems with increasing complexity. The Campden Instruments integration (C137-C139) demonstrates compatibility with commercial systems. The custom mouse touchscreen system (C140-C150) shows full implementation capability. The scalability claim (C148-C150) is directly supported by operational experience with up to 4 systems controlled by one PC.

result: LabNet achieves near real-time hardware control over the network, handling thousands of messages per second in stress tests, with the client (not LabNet) being the performance bottleneck, and successfully executing multiple concurrent tasks without reaching RasPi performance limits in actual experimental use.
evaluation: Claims C152-C153 state the performance capabilities supported by stress test data, C154 identifies the bottleneck through inference from test results, C155 provides real-world validation, and C158-C160 demonstrate multi-tasking capability. The identification of the client as bottleneck (C154) is a reasonable inference from the stress test showing LabNet can handle far more messages than typical experiments require (C155).

result: LabNet's network architecture uses Raspberry Pi nodes (selected for low cost, power, and ecosystem) as servers with a PC client, allowing remote laboratory monitoring, in contrast to Autopilot's hierarchical approach which requires additional configuration and can complicate troubleshooting.
evaluation: Claims C27-C33 describe the rationale for using Raspberry Pi and the resulting network architecture. Claims C34-C36 provide comparison with Autopilot, and C37-C43 detail the specific client-server architecture. The comparison with Autopilot (C34-C36) is somewhat subjective regarding troubleshooting complexity but represents a reasonable design trade-off assessment. The current limitation of one client per server (C43) is honestly acknowledged.

result: LabNet uses Protobuf for message serialization, chosen for performance, small message size, and multi-language support, with a custom solution (type and size prefix in varint notation) to address Protobuf's lack of built-in message framing, following officially recommended practices.
evaluation: Claims C56-C57 and C208-C213 establish the choice of Protobuf and rationale. Claims C219-C226 describe the technical implementation details addressing Protobuf's limitations. The solution (C224-C226) follows official recommendations, lending credibility. The design criteria (C208) are reasonable for the application domain.

result: The Raspberry Pi's multi-core architecture (4 cores since version 2) and asynchronous hardware controllers with DMA motivated LabNet's actor-based architecture to leverage hardware parallelism while avoiding the complexity and error-proneness of traditional multi-threaded programming.
evaluation: Claims C67-C72 describe the hardware characteristics of the Raspberry Pi, C73 identifies the challenge of multi-threaded programming, and C75 states the benefit of the actor model. This represents a coherent design rationale linking hardware capabilities to software architecture choices. The characterization of multi-threaded programming as error-prone (C73) is well-established in software engineering.

result: LabNet uses SObjectizer's actor framework features including simple message/actor definitions, named and unnamed Mboxes for communication, hierarchical state machines for interface actors, and thread pool dispatchers for balancing overhead and parallelism, with flexibility to mix paradigms and change dispatcher types.
evaluation: Claims C184-C207 comprehensively describe SObjectizer's features and how LabNet uses them. These are factual descriptions of the framework's capabilities (verifiable from SObjectizer documentation) and LabNet's implementation choices (C191, C201, C205). The assessment of the thread pool dispatcher as a good compromise (C206) is a reasonable engineering judgment.

result: LabNet's implementation uses TCP/IP via Boost ASIO hidden behind a server actor, with interface actors automatically created by an interface manager, resource management through a resource manager, and a digital output helper actor for complex timing operations like pulses and automatic pin control.
evaluation: Claims C229-C242 describe implementation details of LabNet's actor system. These are straightforward descriptions of the software architecture and division of responsibilities. The automatic reconnection capability (C233) is a useful feature. The separation of simple operations (C239) from complex timing operations (C240-C242) represents good software design.

result: Despite Python's popularity in recent tools (Autopilot, pyControl) and its simplicity and extensive packages, LabNet uses C++ for execution speed, currently requiring recompilation for extensions but with plans for a future plug-in system.
evaluation: Claims C60-C62 establish the trade-off between interpreted and compiled languages, C64-C66 describe the current extension mechanism and future plans. The characterization of interpreted language performance (C60) is well-established. The acknowledgment of current limitations (C65) and future plans (C66) is honest and appropriate for a methods paper.

result: Future LabNet development plans include visual stimuli display, touchscreen support, I2C communication, complete API documentation, Raspberry Pi-based configuration files for automatic hardware initialization, and a plug-in system requiring API rework to support runtime-unknown messages.
evaluation: Claims C166-C173 describe planned future features. These are statements of intent rather than completed work, appropriately presented as future plans. The technical requirements are reasonable (e.g., API rework for plug-in system, C172-C173). However, as these are plans rather than achievements, they cannot be evaluated for scientific validity beyond assessing whether the plans are technically feasible, which they appear to be.

result: Whisker, developed since 1999 at Cambridge, uses a similar client-server architecture to LabNet with TCP/IP communication and plain-text protocol, supporting flexible client implementation in any language, extensive hardware support, and is commercially used in Campden Instruments' ABET II system.
evaluation: Claims C245-C253 describe Whisker's architecture and capabilities, supported by citation to Cardinal and Aitken 2010. The comparison to LabNet (C250) is appropriate for context. The description of Whisker's capabilities is factual and verifiable from the cited literature and commercial product information (C253).

result: pyControl is an open-source framework using MicroPython microcontrollers with modular behavior ports, Python-based finite-state machine task definition, and timestamped event logging, providing sufficient I/O for most tasks but with limitations in hardware types and mandatory state machine structure.
evaluation: Claims C254-C263 describe pyControl's architecture and features, supported by citation to Akam et al. 2022. Claims C264-C266 provide critical assessment of limitations. The assessment of limitations (C265-C266) is fair and balanced, acknowledging both capabilities and constraints. The description is factual and verifiable from pyControl documentation.

result: Bpod, originally from the Brody lab and now maintained by Sanworks, uses Arduino-powered modules for hardware flexibility, MATLAB-based finite-state machine task definition, and transfers state machines to hardware for execution, but is limited to controlling one system per MATLAB session and has restricted software flexibility compared to pyControl or Whisker.
evaluation: Claims C267-C276 describe Bpod's architecture and features, supported by citation to Sanders 2021. Claims C277-C280 identify limitations. The assessment of limitations (C277-C280) is reasonable given the described architecture. The limitation of one Bpod per MATLAB session (C277) is a direct consequence of the design where the state machine is transferred to hardware (C275).

result: Autopilot, developed at University of Oregon, is a Python-based framework for Raspberry Pi using a three-tier agent architecture (terminal, pilot, child) for distributed control, offering the most flexibility among compared tools with extensive hardware support and extensibility, but limited to Python implementation.
evaluation: Claims C281-C295 describe Autopilot's architecture, supported by citation to Saunders and Wehr 2019. Claims C296-C300 provide comparative assessment. The characterization of Autopilot as most flexible (C296) is supported by the described architecture. The limitation to Python (C300) is factual. The description is consistent with Autopilot documentation and published literature.

result: The development of LabNet builds on the authors' 20 years of experience with embedded control systems and 10 years with Raspberry Pi, progressing from PC digital I/O boards (760 lines) to custom microcontrollers to Raspberry Pi adoption in 2015, with the current version representing a 2-year ground-up rebuild of a prior 5-year-old version.
evaluation: Claims C1 and C14 provide context about the broader field, while C15-C16 and C119-C123 describe the authors' specific development trajectory. The progression is logical and supported by citation to Winter and Stich 2005 (C120). This provides important context for understanding LabNet's design decisions but is primarily historical background rather than a scientific result.

result: LabNet was designed with specific goals: time-critical operation, ease of extension, support for diverse hardware, simultaneous control of multiple operant boxes, language-agnostic client implementation, and general applicability to laboratory automation, distinguishing it from complete ecosystems like Autopilot.
evaluation: Claims C17-C26 articulate LabNet's design goals and philosophy. These are statements of intent that shaped the development, with the subsequent technical results (performance, architecture, deployments) providing evidence that these goals were achieved. The distinction from Autopilot (C24) clarifies the scope. Figure 1 (C23) provides visual context for the target applications.

result: The Raspberry Pi OS (Debian-based Linux) provides programming language flexibility, and LabNet currently supports GPIOs, UARTs, audio output, custom HATs, and can integrate with hardware from Bpod, pyControl, MedAssociates, Coulbourn Instruments, and existing systems like Campden Instruments equipment.
evaluation: Claims C58-C59 describe the OS foundation, C161-C163 list currently supported hardware, C164 describes compatibility with other systems, and C165 references demonstrated integration. The hardware support claims are verifiable from the experimental examples provided earlier. The integration with Campden Instruments (C165) is supported by the earlier detailed description (C137-C139).

result: Whisker's typical same-PC deployment achieves extremely fast communication (0.066 ms as reported by authors), with the 1 ms latency in comparisons arising from Whisker's internal 1 kHz polling frequency for processing incoming commands.
evaluation: Claims C110-C112 explain Whisker's performance characteristics. C111 cites the Whisker authors' reported communication speed, and C112 provides the mechanistic explanation for the 1 ms latency. This is important context for the performance comparison, as it explains why Whisker shows 1 ms latency despite very fast network communication. The explanation is consistent with the cited literature.

result: The observed latency decrease from 0.89 ms (one signal) to 0.70 ms (two signals) in stress tests is attributed to increased probability of detecting pin state changes within shorter delays due to polling mechanism and parallel test execution.
evaluation: Claims C98-C99 provide a speculative explanation for an observed phenomenon. While the explanation is plausible (more signals increase the chance of detection within a polling cycle), it is explicitly marked as speculation ("probably") and lacks direct experimental validation. The phenomenon is real (C96-C97) but the mechanistic explanation remains unverified.

result: Very large messages (e.g., video data) could potentially worsen latency of other messages, but this can be mitigated by using separate networks and network cards for camera data.
evaluation: Claims C156-C157 discuss a potential limitation and solution. However, this is speculation about a scenario not tested in the manuscript ("could significantly worsen"). The proposed solution (separate network) is reasonable but also untested. This represents thoughtful consideration of potential issues rather than demonstrated results.

result: LabNet deliberately does not provide support for experimental task design, leaving this responsibility to clients, with hardware initialization currently performed exclusively through client messages without configuration files.
evaluation: Claims C11, C53-C54 describe the design philosophy of separating hardware control from experimental logic, while C227-C228 describe the current implementation approach. This is a clear statement of scope and design decision. The lack of configuration files (C227) is acknowledged as a current limitation with plans for future improvement (C168-C169).

result: The actor model, proposed by Hewitt, Bishop, and Steiger in 1973, uses message-passing between independent actors following shared-nothing and fire-and-forget principles to avoid race conditions and deadlocks, with successful implementations including Erlang (Ericsson, late 1980s) and Akka (2009).
evaluation: Claims C174-C182 provide background on the actor model with appropriate citations (Hewitt et al. 1973, Armstrong 1996, Lightbend 2021). This is established computer science knowledge presented as context for LabNet's architectural choice. The historical information is verifiable from the cited sources and represents accurate characterization of the actor model paradigm.

result: Text-based serialization formats (XML, JSON, ASCII) offer human readability but have disadvantages in message size and computing requirements, while binary formats like Protobuf offer better performance despite not being the most efficient option (compared to Flatbuffers, Cap'n Proto, SBE), with efficiency differences only critical for very large messages or extremely high rates atypical in behavioral experiments.
evaluation: Claims C209-C211 describe text format trade-offs, C214-C217 discuss Protobuf's position among binary formats, and C218 provides domain-specific context. This represents a balanced technical assessment of serialization options. The characterization of when Protobuf's limitations become critical (C217) is reasonable, and the application to behavioral experiments (C218) is a sound inference from typical experimental requirements.

result: Most comparable behavioral experiment control tools are more comprehensive packages offering not just hardware control but also experiment design tools, user interfaces, and data visualization capabilities, unlike LabNet which focuses specifically on hardware control.
evaluation: Claims C243-C244 provide comparative context for LabNet's scope. This is a fair characterization of the landscape of behavioral control software, distinguishing LabNet's focused approach from more comprehensive systems. This context is important for understanding LabNet's design philosophy (C24-C26) and positioning in the field.

result: LabNet source code is available on GitHub under GPL-3.0 license, with performance measurement data, comparison tool implementations, and graph code also available, along with compilation instructions for two paths (Raspberry Pi with VS Code/CMake, or VS 2019 with Docker) and example test code.
evaluation: Claims C301-C306 describe code and data availability. These are factual statements about what is provided in the repository. The availability of code, data, and documentation is essential for reproducibility and represents good open science practice. The provision of multiple compilation paths (C303-C305) facilitates adoption.
